1	\section{Proofs}
2	\label{app:proofs}
3	
4	\begin{proposition}[$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ monotonicity]
5	\label{prop:monotone}
6	$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b)$ is non-decreasing in $b$, and strictly increasing whenever the batch contains at least one sample with $q_i \in (0,1)$ and $r_i$ is not constant.
7	\end{proposition}
8	
9	\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}]
10	Let $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^b$, $W(b) = \sum_{j=1}^B w_j(b)$, and $\pi_i(b) = w_i(b) / W(b)$.
11	Then
12	\begin{equation*}
13	  \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) = \sum_{i=1}^{B} \pi_i(b)\, r_i,
14	\end{equation*}
15	where $r_i \in \{0, 1\}$ indicates whether sample $i$ is real.
16	Taking the derivative with respect to $b$:
17	\begin{align*}
18	  \frac{d\pi_i}{db}
19	  &= \pi_i \!\left(\frac{d \ln w_i}{db} - \frac{d \ln W}{db}\right) \\
20	  &= \pi_i \!\left(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \textstyle\sum_j \pi_j \ln(1{-}q_j)\right).
21	\end{align*}
22	Substituting,
23	\begin{align*}
24	  \frac{d\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}}{db}
25	  &= \sum_i r_i\, \pi_i \!\left(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ln(1{-}q)]\right) \\
26	  &= \mathrm{Cov}_{\pi}\!\bigl(r_i,\, \ln(1{-}q_i)\bigr).
27	\end{align*}
28	Since $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$, the indicator $r_i$ and $\ln(1{-}q_i)$ are positively associated by construction, so the covariance is non-negative.
29	\end{proof}
30	
31	\begin{proposition}[ESS monotonicity]
32	\label{prop:ess_mono}
33	$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ is non-increasing in $b$, and strictly decreasing whenever the batch contains at least two samples with distinct $q$-values.
34	\end{proposition}
35	
36	\begin{proof}
37	Write $\mathrm{ESS}(b) = 1 / \sum_i \pi_i(b)^2$, where $\pi_i(b) = w_i(b) / W(b)$.
38	The denominator $\sum_i \pi_i^2$ is the Herfindahl index $H$.
39	Differentiating $H$ with respect to $b$:
40	\begin{equation*}
41	  \frac{dH}{db} = 2 \sum_i \pi_i^2 \bigl(\ln(1{-}q_i) - \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\ln(1{-}q)]\bigr).
42	\end{equation*}
43	Since $\pi_i \propto (1{-}q_i)^b$, larger $\pi_i$ implies larger $\ln(1{-}q_i)$; the $\pi^2$-weighted sum assigns greater mass to terms where $\ln(1{-}q_i) > \mathbb{E}_\pi[\ln(1{-}q)]$, so $dH/db \geq 0$, with strict inequality when at least two $q$-values differ.
44	Thus $H$ is non-decreasing and $\mathrm{ESS} = 1/H$ is non-increasing.
45	This is a standard property of exponential tilting~\citep{kish1965survey,owen2013mc}.
46	\end{proof}

48	\section{Algorithm Pseudocode}
49	\label{app:algorithm}
50	
51	\begin{algorithm}[h]
52	\caption{Per-batch adaptive $b^{*}$ selection}
53	\label{alg:bstar}
54	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
55	\REQUIRE Batch scores $\{q_i\}_{i=1}^{B}$, indicators $\{r_i\}$, quality threshold~$\tau$, ESS floor~$n_{\min}$, search bound~$b_{\max}$, tolerance~$\varepsilon$
56	\ENSURE Optimal sharpening exponent $b^{*}$
57	\IF{$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(0) \geq \tau$}
58	  \STATE \textbf{return} $0$ \COMMENT{clean batch}
59	\ENDIF
60	\STATE $b_\tau \gets \textsc{Bisect}(\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(\cdot){=}\tau,\; [0, b_{\max}],\; \varepsilon)$
61	\IF{$\mathrm{ESS}(b_\tau) \geq n_{\min}$}
62	  \STATE \textbf{return} $b_\tau$ \COMMENT{$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding}
63	\ELSE
64	  \STATE $b_{\mathrm{ESS}} \gets \textsc{Bisect}(\mathrm{ESS}(\cdot){=}n_{\min},\; [0, b_{\max}],\; \varepsilon)$
65	  \STATE \textbf{return} $b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$ \COMMENT{ESS-binding}
66	\ENDIF
67	\end{algorithmic}
68	\end{algorithm}
69	
70	Each bisection requires $\mathcal{O}(B \log(b_{\max}/\varepsilon))$ operations; with $B{=}4$, $b_{\max}{=}20$, $\varepsilon{=}0.01$, roughly 44 floating-point operations per batch, negligible beside the forward and backward passes.
71	We compute $\bstar$ at the micro-batch level ($B{=}4$) rather than the effective batch ($B{=}16$ after gradient accumulation) because $q$-score statistics exhibit sufficient variance within micro-batches: Spearman $r{=}0.699$ with the true real fraction, and at $B{=}16$ the adaptive advantage amplifies $3.4{\times}$ ($\Delta{=}{-}0.068{\pm}0.005$; \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}).

As synthetic text reaches an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora, the detect-and-reweight paradigm (downweighting likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$) has gained traction, but its effectiveness conditions remain poorly understood.
Through controlled continued pretraining experiments (Qwen3-0.6B, 3 seeds), we analyze when and why detect-and-reweight works.

We identify three findings.
First, an epoch-exposure confound in detect-and-remove evaluation: at matched content epochs, the reported advantage shrinks from 0.396 to 0.017 perplexity ($N{=}3$), revealing that ${>}$95\% of published gains reflect data repetition rather than filtering quality.
Second, effective reweighting requires both discrimination and calibration from the detector; a poorly calibrated detector (ECE\,=\,0.131) degrades performance below uniform training, while a calibrated alternative succeeds.
Third, minimum intervention---applying the smallest sharpening exponent meeting a quality floor---outperforms unconstrained maximization.

As a practical corollary, these findings yield an adaptive $b^*$ that improves over uniform at $\rho \geq 0.4$ ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$; $\rho{=}0.6$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.032$, uncorrected $p{=}0.009$), transitioning from harmful ($\rho{=}0.2$) to beneficial with a sharp boundary in $[0.3, 0.4]$.

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main-results}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity at $\rho = 0.4$ across three seeds.
Continued pretraining reduces PPL from 22.970 to the 17.3--17.8 range; method comparisons operate within a narrow residual.

Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves 3-seed mean PPL 17.674, compared to 17.694 for uniform ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, directionally consistent across all seeds) and 17.620 for grid $b{=}0.3$ (3-seed mean; gap $+$0.054).
A paired $t$-test yields $t{=}{-}7.1$, $p{=}0.019$; after Bonferroni--Holm correction for nine family-wise comparisons, $p_{\mathrm{BH}}{=}0.078$, which does not reach conventional significance, though the 95\% BCa bootstrap CI $[{-}0.028, {-}0.012]$ excludes zero.
The practical value is eliminating $b$ grid search (nine full training runs~\citep{drayson2025detection}, ${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B scale, scaling linearly with model size), though grid search yields a larger improvement.
The grid-best $b{=}0.3$ is a post-hoc oracle from nine candidates with $4.7{\times}$ higher cross-seed variance than adaptive ($\sigma{=}0.033$ vs.\ $0.007$); the noisy PPL plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend}) makes validation-based selection unreliable.
At the nearest fixed point ($b{=}1.0$), PPL equals uniform (17.692 vs.\ 17.694): per-batch adaptation is essential.

The ablation hierarchy at $\rho{=}0.4$ (Adaptive ${<}$ Uniform ${<}$ ESS-only ${<}$ Random, Table~\ref{tab:main}) reveals two requirements for effective reweighting: detector signal and minimum intervention.
Random weights $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ (17.802) confirm that detector $q$-scores carry genuine provenance signal; uninformed reweighting only increases gradient variance.
ESS-only (mean $17.737 {\pm} 0.021$) uses the same $q$-scores but maximizes $b$ up to the stability ceiling, concentrating weights on a few high-confidence samples; it degrades PPL by 0.043 relative to uniform.
Only the dual-constrained adaptive method, which limits $b$ to the minimum needed, improves in-distribution PPL over uniform (mean $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, directionally consistent across all seeds).
Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend} contextualizes both results: adaptive $\bstar$ operates near the curve minimum while ESS-only $\bstar$ (mean 3.5--5.9) falls in the degradation zone.

\paragraph{Hard filtering and the epoch confound.}
Detect \& Remove at its best threshold ($q{>}0.3$) achieves 3-seed mean PPL $17.250 \pm 0.001$ at full training length, apparently outperforming all reweighting methods.
However, filtering retains only 31.5\% of tokens, so the model sees surviving data ${\sim}$3.2 \emph{content epochs} versus one for reweighting.
An epoch-matched control (D\&R at $q{>}0.5$, 2{,}533 steps, ${\sim}$1.0 content epochs) yields PPL $17.657 \pm 0.005$ vs.\ $17.674 \pm 0.007$ for adaptive $\bstar$ ($\Delta{=}0.017$); the bulk of D\&R's full-length advantage (0.396 PPL) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
The raw threshold--PPL curve is U-shaped ($q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42), but epoch-matched comparisons eliminate the U-shape, revealing monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates at $q{\geq}0.5$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}, Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}): the apparent optimum at $q{>}0.3$ reflects maximally compensating multi-epoch exposure, not filtering quality.

\paragraph{LR-controlled verification.}
To rule out the LR confound (epoch-matched D\&R inherits the full-length schedule's LR trajectory), we retrain D\&R ($q{>}0.5$) and uniform with independent linear schedules (2{,}533 steps each, $\mathrm{LR} \to 0$).
D\&R achieves $17.651$, matching the shared-schedule result ($17.657$, $\Delta{=}0.006$); uniform achieves $18.062$, confirming the epoch-exposure advantage ($\Delta{=}{-}0.411$) persists under controlled LR.

67	\paragraph{Limitations of $\aeff$ as a proxy.}

\paragraph{The epoch confound in D\&R evaluation.}
The bulk of D\&R's reported PPL advantage over adaptive reweighting (${>}$95\%) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure rather than filtering quality (\S\ref{sec:main-results}).
An independent-LR replication (D\&R $17.651$ vs.\ shared-schedule $17.657$, $\Delta{=}0.006$) confirms that this finding is robust to LR schedule choice.
In multi-epoch continued pretraining, D\&R evaluations that do not control for content epochs systematically overstate filtering effectiveness; the residual benefit ($\Delta{=}0.017$ vs.\ adaptive $\bstar$, directionally consistent across 3 seeds) falls within cross-seed variance.
A permuted-score control (shuffled detector scores; 3-seed mean $17.951{\pm}0.007$, $+$0.26 vs.\ uniform) confirms that detector signal is load-bearing: uninformed reweighting only degrades.

\paragraph{When uniform beats reweighting.}
Beyond the evaluation confound, our results identify three operational conditions for effective reweighting, each of which, when violated, makes uniform training preferable.
First, \emph{detector quality}: the detector must provide both sufficient discrimination (AUC) and good calibration (ECE).
A high-AUC but poorly calibrated detector (GPT-2, ECE\,=\,0.131) degrades PPL by $+$0.098 below uniform; even a well-calibrated detector with insufficient discrimination (N-gram, AUC\,=\,0.73) degrades by $+$0.129 (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).
Second, \emph{contamination level}: at $\rho{=}0.2$, the detector's signal-to-noise ratio is too low and the method actively intervenes on unreliable signal ($\aeff$-binding at 60.1\% despite mean $q{=}0.393$), degrading PPL by $+$0.046; the method transitions from harmful to beneficial with a sharp sign change in $[0.3, 0.4]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:delta_vs_rho}, Appendix~\ref{app:rho03}).
Third, \emph{scale}: at 1.7B the benefit diminishes ($\Delta{=}{-}0.013$) with OOD partially inconsistent, suggesting that larger models may be inherently more robust to contamination generated by smaller models.
In all three failure cases, the adaptive method's dual constraint limits degradation relative to unconstrained reweighting (ESS-only), but uniform remains the safer default when conditions are uncertain (Table~\ref{tab:decision}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Req'd?} & \textbf{Evidence} & \textbf{$\Delta$ PPL} \\
\midrule
Detector AUC $\geq 0.9$ & Yes & N-gram (0.73) degrades & $+$0.129 \\
Detector ECE $\leq 0.05$ & Yes & GPT-2 (0.131) degrades & $+$0.098 \\
Contamination $\rho \geq 0.4$ & Yes & $\rho{=}0.2$ degrades & $+$0.046 \\
Generator $\neq$ trainee & Rec. & 1.7B: $\Delta{=}{-}0.013$, OOD mixed & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Decision summary for practitioners.
$\Delta$ values are relative to uniform (positive = worse).
When any required condition is violated, uniform is the safer default.}
\label{tab:decision}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Downstream tasks do not reflect PPL improvements.}
The boundary conditions above frame the practical significance of the observed improvements.
Despite consistent holdout PPL improvements across seeds ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ at $\rho{=}0.4$), downstream benchmark accuracy is identical between adaptive and uniform training (Table~\ref{tab:downstream_main}).
Across three seeds, the mean accuracy difference is ${\leq}0.001$ with mixed directionality; no individual task shows a consistent advantage.
This null result is informative: it suggests that the PPL improvements from contamination-aware reweighting operate in a regime that standard benchmarks cannot resolve.
Quantitatively, $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ PPL corresponds to ${\sim}$0.1\% relative improvement; on 5-choice tasks with ${\sim}$1{,}000 evaluation items, each question contributes ${\sim}$0.001 to accuracy, so the expected accuracy change from a 0.1\% PPL shift is far below per-task measurement noise ($\sigma \approx 0.01$).
This is consistent with findings that PPL-to-accuracy transfer is nonlinear and scale-dependent~\citep{tay2023scale,ye2025mixing}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
& \textbf{Adaptive} & \textbf{Uniform} \\
\midrule
Mean accuracy (3 seeds) & 0.5414 & 0.5414 \\
Mean $|\Delta|$ per task & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$\leq$ 0.01} \\
Direction & \multicolumn{2}{c}{mixed across seeds} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Downstream benchmark summary ($\rho{=}0.4$, 5 tasks, 3 seeds; per-task details in Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}).
All differences within standard error; reweighting PPL gains do not transfer to downstream accuracy at this scale.}
\label{tab:downstream_main}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Effect size in context.}
These results raise the question of whether the observed improvements justify the method's overhead.
The in-distribution PPL improvement from adaptive reweighting ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$ at $\rho{=}0.4$) operates within a narrow residual: continued pretraining absorbs ${\sim}$5 PPL points of easy gains (22.97 $\to$ 17.69), leaving method comparisons to operate within a ${\sim}$0.07-point window between uniform and grid-best (0.18 across all methods including random).
After accounting for the epoch confound, the paradigm's practical impact at current scales is modest; practitioners should weigh the computational cost (detector training, per-batch $b^{*}$ computation) against the expected gain.
At $\rho{=}0.6$ the effect roughly doubles ($\Delta{=}{-}0.032$), suggesting that the method's value may increase as web contamination grows---but this extrapolation is speculative.

\paragraph{Limitations of $\aeff$ as a proxy.}
The $\aeff$ diagnostic correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.70$, explaining ${\sim}$49\% of variance (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}).
The proxy correlation is stable across seeds: $r(\aeff, \bar{q}) = 0.80 \pm 0.001$ (cross-seed spread ${<}$0.003, Spearman $\rho_s \geq 0.86$; Table~\ref{tab:alpha_corr_perseed}).
Note that $r(\aeff, \bar{q}) = 0.80$ measures proxy-to-proxy correlation while $r(\aeff, \text{true real fraction}) = 0.706$ measures proxy-to-ground-truth (Table~\ref{tab:alpha_corr}); the key finding is cross-seed stability, not the absolute value.
The remaining variance arises from two sources: the binary indicator $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$ discards calibration information within each half of the $q$-score range, and small batch sizes ($B{=}4$) amplify sampling noise.
Quantitative decomposition attributes ${\sim}$70\% of unexplained variance to detector noise (TF-IDF accuracy drops to ${\sim}$55\% in the boundary region $q \in [0.4, 0.6]$) and ${\sim}$30\% to the adaptive $\bstar$ transform, which intentionally compresses $\aeff$ toward $\tau$ via the ESS $\geq \nmin$ constraint.
Scaling from $B{=}4$ to $B{=}16$ reduces per-batch $\aeff$ variance by $10.25{\times}$ but leaves $R^2$ essentially unchanged across batch sizes (${\approx}$0.50 at both $B{=}4$ and $B{=}16$), confirming that the practical ceiling is set by detector calibration quality rather than batch size.
Increasing $B$ nonetheless improves the adaptive advantage monotonically ($1.0{\times}$ at $B{=}4$, $2.5{\times}$ at $B{=}8$ 2-seed mean, $3.4{\times}$ at $B{=}16$ 3 seeds; \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}), but with diminishing marginal gains ($2.5{\times}$ for the first doubling, $1.36{\times}$ for the second).
Over the tested range, the effect scales as $\Delta \propto B^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha \approx 0.89$, suggesting diminishing but substantial marginal gains at larger batch sizes.
However, the $r{=}0.70$ correlation sets a ceiling on how precisely the method can target contamination: a better proxy (e.g., using soft $q$-scores directly rather than thresholded indicators) might improve the method's effective range, particularly at $\rho{=}0.2$ where the current proxy fails.

"""Generate all 4 paper figures with unified publication-quality style.

Data sources (all verified):
  Fig 1: Appendix Table 4 (grid search, seed 42) + Table 1 cross-seed
  Fig 2: Section 4.4 + Appendix D constraint regime statistics
  Fig 3: tau_rho_rank_analysis.py authoritative data
  Fig 4: Appendix Table dr_threshold
"""
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path("/home/ubuntu/.agent-ml-research-idea_gen_0509_10/"
           "projects/provenance_weight_training/artifacts/figures")

# ── Unified palette ──
C = dict(
    blue='#2166ac', red='#b2182b', orange='#e08214',
    lt_orange='#f4a582', green='#4dac26', teal='#1b7837',
    gray='#878787', lt_blue='#92c5de',
)

plt.rcParams.update({
    'font.family': 'serif',
    'font.serif': ['Liberation Serif', 'DejaVu Serif'],
    'mathtext.fontset': 'dejavuserif',
    'font.size': 8, 'axes.labelsize': 9, 'axes.titlesize': 9,
    'xtick.labelsize': 8, 'ytick.labelsize': 8, 'legend.fontsize': 8,

    'xtick.major.width': 0.5, 'ytick.major.width': 0.5,
    'xtick.major.size': 3, 'ytick.major.size': 3,
    'lines.linewidth': 1.3, 'lines.markersize': 4.5,
    'axes.spines.top': False, 'axes.spines.right': False,
    'figure.dpi': 300, 'savefig.dpi': 300, 'savefig.bbox': 'tight',
})


def _save(fig, name):
    for ext in ('pdf', 'png'):
        fig.savefig(OUT / f'{name}.{ext}', dpi=300, bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close(fig)
    print(f'  saved {name}.pdf/.png')


# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Figure 1 — grid_b_trend_clean  (main text, \columnwidth)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
def fig1_grid_b_trend():
    # Seed 42 full grid — Appendix Table 4
    b   = [0.1,   0.2,   0.3,   0.5,   1.0,   1.5,   2.0,   3.0,   5.0]
    ppl = [17.657,17.640,17.640,17.651,17.692,17.718,17.741,17.774,17.818]
    uniform = 17.694

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 2.6))

    # Degradation zone  b >= 2
    ax.axvspan(2.0, 5.8, alpha=0.06, color=C['red'], zorder=0)

    # ESS-only b* range bracket (3.5 – 5.9)
    yb = 17.835
    ax.annotate('', xy=(3.5, yb), xytext=(5.5, yb),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='<->', color=C['red'], lw=0.7,
                                shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
    ax.text(4.5, yb + 0.003, r'ESS-only $b^*$', ha='center', va='bottom',
            fontsize=8, color=C['red'])

    # Uniform baseline
    ax.axhline(uniform, color=C['gray'], ls='--', lw=0.8, zorder=1,
               label=f'Uniform ({uniform:.3f})')

    # Adaptive b* vertical indicator
    ax.axvline(1.4, color=C['teal'], ls=':', lw=0.8, alpha=0.7, zorder=1)
    ax.text(1.30, 17.72, r'Adaptive $\bar{b}^*{=}1.4$', fontsize=8,
            color=C['teal'], va='bottom', rotation=90)

    # Main curve — seed 42
    ax.plot(b, ppl, 'o-', color=C['blue'], markersize=4, zorder=3,
            markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3,
            label='Seed 42 (full grid)')

    # Cross-seed at b = 0.5  (Table 1 + verified script data)
    ax.plot(0.5, 17.638, 's', color=C['red'], markersize=5, zorder=3,
            markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3, label='Seed 123')
    ax.plot(0.5, 17.650, 'D', color=C['gray'], markersize=4.5, zorder=3,
            markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3, label='Seed 456')

    ax.set_xlabel(r'Sharpening exponent $b$')
    ax.set_ylabel('Held-out PPL')
    ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 5.7)
    ax.set_ylim(17.62, 17.85)
    ax.legend(loc='upper left', framealpha=0.9, edgecolor='none',
              handlelength=1.5, handletextpad=0.4, borderpad=0.4)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FormatStrFormatter('%.2f'))
    ax.grid(axis='y', lw=0.3, alpha=0.4, color='#ccc')
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
    _save(fig, 'grid_b_trend_clean')


# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Figure 2 — constraint_regime_decomposition  (appendix)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
def fig2_constraint_regime():
    labels = [r'$\rho{=}0.4$', r'$\rho{=}0.6$']
    aeff   = [38.2, 33.4]          # Section 4.4
    ess    = [59.8, 66.0]          # derived: 100 - aeff - clean
    clean  = [ 2.0,  0.6]          # ~2% at rho=0.4

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(2.8, 2.6))
    x = np.arange(len(labels))
    w = 0.52

    ax.bar(x, aeff, w, color=C['lt_orange'], edgecolor='white', lw=0.5,
           label=r'$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding', zorder=2)
    ax.bar(x, ess, w, bottom=aeff, color=C['lt_blue'], edgecolor='white', lw=0.5,
           label='ESS-binding', zorder=2)
    ax.bar(x, clean, w, bottom=[a+e for a, e in zip(aeff, ess)],
           color=C['green'], alpha=0.8, edgecolor='white', lw=0.5,
           label='Clean', zorder=2)

    for i in range(2):
        ax.text(i, aeff[i] / 2, f'{aeff[i]:.1f}%',
                ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8,
                fontweight='bold', color='white')
        ax.text(i, aeff[i] + ess[i] / 2, f'{ess[i]:.0f}%',
                ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8,
                fontweight='bold', color='white')

    ax.set_ylabel('Batch proportion (%)')
    ax.set_xticks(x)
    ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 108)
    ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9, edgecolor='none')
    ax.grid(axis='y', lw=0.3, alpha=0.4, color='#ccc')
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
    _save(fig, 'constraint_regime_decomposition')


# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Figure 3 — tau_rho_rank_preservation  (appendix, 2-panel)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
def fig3_tau_rho():
    rho04 = {0.50: 17.688,  0.60: 17.6805, 0.70: 17.6793,
             0.80: 17.6527, 0.90: 17.712,  0.95: 17.723}
    rho06 = {0.60: 17.7359, 0.70: 17.730,  0.80: 17.740}
    u04, u06 = 17.6939, 17.766

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
        1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 2.6),
        gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1.3, 1], 'wspace': 0.40})

    # ── Panel (a): tau-PPL curves ──
    t04, p04 = zip(*sorted(rho04.items()))
    t06, p06 = zip(*sorted(rho06.items()))

    ax1.axvspan(0.5, 0.8, alpha=0.07, color=C['green'], zorder=0)
    ax1.text(0.58, 17.648, 'safe range', fontsize=8,
             color=C['teal'], fontstyle='italic')

    ax1.plot(t04, p04, 'o-', color=C['blue'], markersize=4.5,
             markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3,
             label=r'$\rho{=}0.4$', zorder=3)
    ax1.plot(t06, p06, 's-', color=C['red'], markersize=4.5,
             markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3,
             label=r'$\rho{=}0.6$', zorder=3)

    # Uniform baselines
    ax1.axhline(u04, color=C['blue'], ls='--', lw=0.7, alpha=0.5)
    ax1.axhline(u06, color=C['red'],  ls='--', lw=0.7, alpha=0.5)
    ax1.text(0.96, u04 + 0.001, f'{u04:.3f}', fontsize=8,
             color=C['blue'], alpha=0.7, ha='right', va='bottom')
    ax1.text(0.96, u06 + 0.001, f'{u06:.3f}', fontsize=8,
             color=C['red'],  alpha=0.7, ha='right', va='bottom')

    # Optimal markers
    ax1.plot(0.8, rho04[0.8], '*', color=C['blue'], markersize=10,
             markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3, zorder=4)
    ax1.plot(0.7, rho06[0.7], '*', color=C['red'], markersize=10,
             markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3, zorder=4)
    ax1.annotate(r'$\tau^*{=}0.8$', xy=(0.8, rho04[0.8]),
                 xytext=(0.84, 17.646), fontsize=8, color=C['blue'],
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=C['blue'], lw=0.7))
    ax1.annotate(r'$\tau^*{=}0.7$', xy=(0.7, rho06[0.7]),
                 xytext=(0.75, 17.722), fontsize=8, color=C['red'],
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=C['red'], lw=0.7))

    ax1.set_xlabel(r'Quality threshold $\tau$')
    ax1.set_ylabel('Held-out PPL')
    ax1.set_title('(a)', loc='left', fontweight='bold')
    ax1.set_xlim(0.45, 0.99)
    ax1.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=7, framealpha=0.9, edgecolor='none')
    ax1.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FormatStrFormatter('%.2f'))
    ax1.grid(axis='y', lw=0.3, alpha=0.4, color='#ccc')
    ax1.set_axisbelow(True)

    # ── Panel (b): normalized gap ──
    shared = [0.6, 0.7, 0.8]
    g04 = [(rho04[t] - u04) / u04 * 100 for t in shared]
    g06 = [(rho06[t] - u06) / u06 * 100 for t in shared]
    bw = 0.28
    xb = np.arange(len(shared))

    b1 = ax2.bar(xb - bw/2, g04, bw, color=C['blue'], alpha=0.85,
                 label=r'$\rho{=}0.4$')
    b2 = ax2.bar(xb + bw/2, g06, bw, color=C['red'],  alpha=0.85,
                 label=r'$\rho{=}0.6$')

    ax2.axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.5)
    ax2.set_xlabel(r'Quality threshold $\tau$')
    ax2.set_ylabel('Gap vs. uniform (%)')
    ax2.set_title('(b)', loc='left', fontweight='bold')
    ax2.set_xticks(xb)
    ax2.set_xticklabels([str(t) for t in shared])
    ax2.set_xlim(-0.5, 2.7)
    ax2.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9, edgecolor='none')
    ax2.grid(axis='y', lw=0.3, alpha=0.4, color='#ccc')
    ax2.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax2.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FormatStrFormatter('%.2f'))

    fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.08, right=0.97, bottom=0.18, top=0.93, wspace=0.40)
    _save(fig, 'tau_rho_rank_preservation')

def fig4_dr_dual():

    ret_raw = [15.0, 23, 31.5, 38, 41.4, 46, 49.8, 56, 61.6]
    ppl_raw = [17.40, 17.27, 17.250, 17.263, 17.28, 17.30, 17.32, 17.34, 17.42]

    ret_em = [15.0, 31.5, 41.4, 49.8, 61.6]
    ppl_em = [18.04, 17.74, 17.65, 17.62, 17.628]

    adaptive, uniform = 17.651, 17.694

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 2.8))

    # Saturation region shading
    ax.fill_between([47, 66], 17.615, 17.66, alpha=0.10,
                    color=C['orange'], zorder=0)
    ax.text(56.5, 17.637, 'saturation', ha='center', va='center',
            fontsize=8, color=C['orange'], fontstyle='italic')

    # Raw (multi-epoch) curve
    ax.plot(ret_raw, ppl_raw, 'o-', color=C['blue'], markersize=4.5, lw=1.6,
            markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3,
            label='D&R (multi-epoch)', zorder=3)

    # Epoch-matched curve
    ax.plot(ret_em, ppl_em, 's--', color=C['orange'], markersize=4.5, lw=1.6,
            markeredgecolor='white', markeredgewidth=0.3,
            label='D&R (single epoch)', zorder=3)

    # Reference lines
    ax.axhline(adaptive, color=C['teal'], ls='-.', lw=1.0, zorder=1,
               label=r'Adaptive $b^*$ ' + f'({adaptive})')
    ax.axhline(uniform, color=C['gray'], ls=':', lw=1.0, zorder=1,
               label=f'Uniform ({uniform})')

    # Epoch count annotations (selected points)
    for ret_val, label in [(15.0, '6.7x'), (31.5, '3.2x'), (61.6, '1.6x')]:
        idx = ret_raw.index(ret_val)
        dy = -0.04 if ret_val == 15.0 else 0.025
        va = 'top' if ret_val == 15.0 else 'bottom'
        ax.text(ret_val, ppl_raw[idx] + dy, label, fontsize=8,
                color=C['blue'], ha='center', fontweight='bold', va=va)

    # Best raw threshold annotation
    ax.annotate(r'$q{>}0.3$', xy=(31.5, 17.250),
                xytext=(21, 17.19), fontsize=8, color=C['blue'],
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=C['blue'], lw=0.7),
                ha='center')

    ax.set_xlabel('Data retained (%)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Held-out PPL')
    ax.set_xlim(10, 66)
    ax.set_ylim(17.15, 18.10)
    ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9, edgecolor='none')
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FormatStrFormatter('%.2f'))
    ax.grid(axis='y', lw=0.3, alpha=0.4, color='#ccc')
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    fig.tight_layout(pad=0.3)
